newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serb opposition takes over Belgrade council.
newsitem.headline: Serb opposition takes over Belgrade council.

text.p: Serbia's opposition coalition took control of Belgrade's council on Friday after winning a three-month battle with ruling socialists to get them to recognise opposition wins in local elections last November.
The three-party Zajedno (Together) coalition, which now holds 67 out of 110 seats in the assembly, proposed one of its co-leaders, Zoran Djindjic, for mayor.

He was the only candidate and was expected to win easily, but opposition delegates from the Serbian Radical Party held up the vote, telling the chamber they were opposed to Djindjic's election because of a conviction for petty theft.
He is alleged to have stolen a book when he was a student.
They also said Belgrade University students, who are still demonstrating daily for the removal of their rector, were under Djindjic's direct control.
A rally was due to be held on Friday evening in the city centre to celebrate the opposition victory despite controversy among the members of the coalition.
One of Zajedno's co-leaders Vuk Draskovic demanded radical changes to the rally programme before he agreed to attend.

"Pledges, fireworks, trumpets and drums, spectacle and strong words stand in stark contrast to our unpretentious resistance to stealing and to brutal force, and they are also in stark contrast to the grim reality of Belgrade and the whole of Serbia," his Serbian Renewal Movement said in a statement.
"The hungry are still in the streets, and there will be many more of them. The students are still protesting...What do we have to celebrate?" said Draskovic's party.

Zajedno called off its street protests, which had involved half a million people at their height, after President Slobodan Milosevic's socialists recognised their victories, but leaders say two key goals remain to be met.
Zajedno now wants the authoritarian government to free the country's heavily-controlled media and to create fair conditions for parliamentary and presidential elections due later this year.
In Serbia's centralised system the state-run television and radio is used to keep Milosevic in power.
